raw_text:
{{RunningHeader|Triumfetta|6492|triumvirate}}{{smaller|tralia, Madagascar, or South Africa. A group of American species produces large dense masses of showy cymulose flowers. The fruit is two- to five-celled, and separates into distinct carpels, or is indehiscent and bur-like, its prickles often ending in hooks, as in ''T. Lappula'', a common tropical weed known in Jamaica as ''greatwort''. The species in general are known in the West Indies as ''burweed'' or ''parrakeet-bur'', the ripe fruit being a favorite food of the green parrakeet. Several species are used medicinally in the tropics on account of their mucilaginous properties; several also yield a tenacious fiber, as ''T. rhomboidea'', a wide-spread tropical weed, and ''T. semitriloba'' (for which see ''bur-bark'').}} '''triumph''' (trī′umf), ''n.'' [< ME. ''triumphe'', ''tryumphe'', < OF. ''triumphe'', ''triomphe'', F. ''triomphe'' = Pr. ''triomfe'' = Sp. ''triunfo'' = Pg. ''triumpho'' = It. ''trionfo'', ''triunfo'' = D. ''triomf'', ''triumf'' = G. ''triumph'' = Sw. Dan. ''triumf'', triumph (in OF. and It. also a game of cards so called), < L. ''triumphus'', OL. ''triumpus'', in the earliest use ''triumpe'', ''triumpe'', ''triumpe'', an exclamation used in the solemn processions of the Arval brethren; in classical use a solemn entrance in procession, made by a victorious general (see def.), accompanied by the shout ''Io triumphe!'' hence fig. a victory, triumph; = Gr. θρίαμβος, the procession at the feast of Bacchus, also a name for Bacchus; ult. origin unknown. Hence ''trump''3.] '''1.''' In ''Rom. antiq.'', a procession and religious ceremony in honor of a victory and the victorious leader. {{smaller|This, the highest military honor which a Roman commander could attain, was granted by the senate to such as, holding the office of dictator, consul, or pretor, had secured a decisive victory or the complete subjugation of a province. In the triumph}} {{smaller block|''Tarocchi'', a kinde of playing cardes vsed in Italy, calle terrestriall ''triumphes'' [var. called ''Tarocks'', or terestrial ''triumphs'', 1611]. {{right|''Florio'', 1598}}}} '''To ride triumph''', to be in full career; ride rough-shod. {{smaller block|"'Tis some misfortune," quoth my uncle Toby. "That it is," cried my father, "to have so many jarring elements breaking loose, and ''riding triumph'' in every corner of a gentleman's house." {{right|''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, iii. 157. (''Davies''.)}}}} =Syn. 5. ''Joy'', ''Delight'', etc. (see ''gladness''), jubilee, jubilation. '''triumph''' (trī′umf, formerly also trī-umf′), ''v.'' [< F. ''triompher'' = Pr. ''triomfar'' = Sp. ''triunfar'' = Pg. ''triumphar'' = It. ''trionfare'', ''triunfare'', < L. ''triumphare'', < ''triumphus'', a triumph: see ''triumph'', ''n.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To enjoy a triumph as a victorious general; ride in a triumph; celebrate successful achievement. {{smaller block|Wouldst thou have laugh'd had I come coffin'd home, That weep'st to see me ''triumph?'' ''Shak.'', Cor., ii. 1. 194.}} {{smaller block|We wear The dignity of Christians on our breasts, And have a long time ''triumph'd'' for our conquests; These conquer'd a long time, not ''triumph'd'' yet. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Malta, i. 1.}}}} '''2.''' To gain a victory; achieve success; prevail. {{smaller block|He did but climb the cross, and then came down To the gates of hell; ''triumph'd'', and fetch'd a crown. {{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, v. 3., Epig.}}}} {{smaller block|Attired with stars, we shall for ever sit ''Triumphing'' over Death, and Chance, and thee, O Time. {{right|''Milton'', On Time, l. 22.}}}} '''3.''' To rejoice for victory; exult or boast. {{smaller block|the general, crowned with laurel, and having a scepter in one hand and a branch of laurel in the other, entered the city of Rome in a chariot drawn by four horses, preceded by the senate and magistrates, musicians, the spoils, the captives in fetters, etc., and followed by his army on foot, in marching order. The procession advanced in this order along the Via Sacra to the Capitol, where a bull was sacrificed to Jupiter and the laurel wreath was deposited in the lap of the god. Banquets and other entertainments concluded the solemnity, which was generally brought to a close in one day, though in later times it sometimes lasted for three days. During the time of the empire the emperor himself was the only person who could claim a triumph. A naval triumph differed in no respect from a military triumph, except that it was on a smaller scale, and was marked by the exhibition of beaks of ships and other nautical trophies. An ovation was an honor inferior to a triumph, and less imposing in its ceremonies.}} {{smaller block|If we lose this battle,
You are contented to be led in ''triumph''
Thorough the streets of Rome? {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., v. 1. 109.}}}} {{smaller block|Though ''triumphs'' were to generals only due,
Crowns were reserv'd to grace the soldiers too. {{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 512.}}}} {{smaller block|Let not mine enemies ''triumph'' over me. Ps. xxv. 2.}} {{smaller block|How will he ''triumph'', leap, and laugh at it! {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iv. 3. 148.}}}} 4†. To take a trick; trump. {{smaller block|Except the four knaves entertain'd for the guards
Of the kings and queens that ''triumph'' in the cards. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Fortunate Isles.}}}} 5. To shine forth; make a brilliant show. {{smaller block|The clear unmatched red and white
Which ''triumph'd'' in that sky of his delight. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 12.}}}} II.† ''trans.'' 1. To succeed in overcoming; prevail over; subdue; conquer. {{smaller block|Two and thirty legions that awe
All nations of the ''triumph'd'' world. ''Massinger.''}} 2. To cause to triumph; give victory to. {{smaller block|He hath ''triumphed'' the name of his Christ; he will bless the things he hath begun. {{right|''Bp. Jewell'', Works (Parker Soc.), II. 933.}}}} 3. To exult over; boast over. {{smaller block|So oft they fell}} '''2†.''' A public festivity or display of any kind, as an exhibition of masks; a tournament, stately procession, or pageant; a spectacle. {{smaller block|We retournyd ayen to Venys, whiche day was a grete ''tryumphe'' and Feste there in remembraũce of a Victorye that the Venycyans had ye same day in gettynge of Padowa. {{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 7.}}}} {{smaller block|You cannot have a perfect palace except you have two several sides, . . . the one for feasts and ''triumphs'', and the other for dwelling. {{right|''Bacon'', Building (ed. 1887).}}}} '''3.''' The state of being victorious; the flush of victory. {{smaller block|The avenging force of Hercules, from Spain, Arrived in ''triumph'', from Geryon slain. {{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, viii. 267.}}}} {{smaller block|Hail to the Chief who in ''triumph'' advances! {{right|''Scott'', L. of the L., ii. 19.}}}} '''4.''' Successful enterprise or consummation; achievement; conquest. {{smaller block|With Death she humbly doth insinuate; Tells him of trophies, statues, tombs, and stories His victories, his ''triumphs'', and his glories. {{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 1014.}}}} {{smaller block|All the ''triumphs'' of truth and genius over prejudice and power, in every country and in every age, have been the ''triumphs'' of Athens. {{right|''Macaulay'', Mitford's Hist. Greece.}}}} '''5.''' Joy or exultation for success; great gladness; rejoicing. {{smaller block|Great ''triumph'' and rejoicing was in heaven.}} {{smaller block|Into the same illusion, not as man, Whom they ''triumph'd'', once laps'd. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., x. 572.}}}} '''triumphal''' (trī-um′fal), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< F. ''triomphal'' = Sp. ''triunfal'' = Pg. ''triumphal'' = It. ''triunfale'', ''trionfale'', < L. ''triumphalis'', pertaining to a triumph, < ''triumphus'', a triumph: see ''triumph''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to triumph; commemorating or used in celebrating a triumph or victory: as, a ''triumphal'' crown or car; a ''triumphal'' march. {{smaller block|On Ascension day the Duke . . . is rowed thither in the Bucentoro, a ''triumphall'' galley, richly and exquisitely guilded. {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Who [mighty men] have led Kings in chains after their ''Triumphal'' Chariots, and have been served by those whom others have adored. {{right|''Stillingfleet'', Sermons, II. iii.}}}} {{smaller|'''Triumphal arch.''' See ''arch''1.—'''Triumphal column''', among the Romans, an insulated column erected in commemoration of a conqueror to whom had been decreed the honors of a triumph. It has been imitated in a few instances in modern times, as in the bronze column of the Place Vendôme in Paris, set up in honor of Napoleon I.—'''Triumphal crown''', a laurel wreath awarded by the Romans to a victorious general.—'''Triumphal Hymn.''' Same as ''Sanctus'', 1.}} '''II.''' ''n.'' '''1†.''' A token of victory. {{smaller block|So, struck with dread and anguish, fell the fiend; And to his crew, that sat consulting, brought (Joyless ''triumphals'' of his hoped success) Ruin, and desperation, and dismay. {{right|''Milton'', P. R., iv. 578. ''Milton'', P. L., vii. 180.}}}} {{smaller block|If a civilized nation, or any men who had a sense of generosity, were capable of a personal ''triumph'' over the fallen and afflicted.{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}} 6†. A card of a suit which outranks all others; a trump. See ''trump''3, 1. {{smaller block|You must mark also that the ''triumph'' must apply to fetch home unto him all the other cards, whatsoever suit they be of.{{right|''Latimer'', Sermons on the Card (Parker Soc.), i.}}}} {{smaller block|She, Eros, has
Pack'd cards with Cæsar, and false-play'd my glory
Unto an enemy's ''triumph.''{{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., iv. 14. 20.}}}} 7†. An old game of cards, from which whist is probably derived; trump. See ''ruff''4 and ''trump''3, 2. {{smaller block|The game that we will play at shall be called the ''triumph'', which if it be well played at, he that dealeth shall win.{{right|''Latimer'', Sermons on the Card (Parker Soc.), i.}}}} 8†. See the quotation and ''tarot.'' 2. An ode or song in celebration of victory or of peace; a pæan; a hymn of rejoicing. {{smaller block|Those [rejoicings] of victorie and peace are called ''Triumphall'', whereof we our selues haue heretofore giuen some example by our ''Triumphals'' written in honour of her Maiesties long peace.{{right|''Puttenham'', Arte of Eng. Poesie, p. 37.}}}} {{smaller block|Man, if ''triumphals'' here be in request,
Then let them chaunt them that can chaunt them best.{{right|''Peele'', An Eclogue.}}}} '''triumphant''' (trī-um′fant), ''a.'' [< F. ''triomphant'' = Sp. ''triunfante'' = Pg. ''triumphante'' = It. ''triunfante, trionfante'', < L. ''triumphan(t-)s'', ppr. of ''triumphare'', triumph: see ''triumph, v.''] 1†. Celebrating victory by a triumph, as a successful Roman general; also, used in, pertaining to, or appropriate to a triumph; triumphal. {{smaller block|Praise the gods,
And make ''triumphant'' fires; strew flowers before them.{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., v. 5. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|The King rideth on a ''triumphant'' cart or wagon all gilded. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', II. i. 236.}}}} {{smaller block|The streets so broad that tenne men may ride in front, and paued, adorned with many ''triumphant'' Arches, and shops on both sides. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 436.}}}} 2. Rejoicing for or as for victory; triumphing; exulting. {{smaller block|Think you, but that I know our state secure, I would be so ''triumphant'' as I am? {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 2. 84.}}}} 3. Victorious; successful; graced with conquest. {{smaller block|His noble hand Did win what he did spend, and spent not that Which his ''triumphant'' father's hand had won. {{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1. 181.}}}} {{smaller block|He had slain men with his own hand, for aught I know; —certainly, they had fallen, like blades of grass at the sweep of the scythe, before the charge to which his spirit imparted its ''triumphant'' energy. {{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 24.}}}} 4. Of supreme magnificence and beauty; glorious. {{smaller block|She 's a most ''triumphant'' lady, if report be square to her. {{right|''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 2. 189.}}}} '''Church triumphant.''' See ''church.'' '''triumphantly''' (trī-um′fant-li), ''adv.'' 1. In a triumphant manner; in the manner of a victor; with the joy or exultation that proceeds from victory; victoriously: often implying insolent triumph. {{smaller block|Or did I bragge and boast ''triumphauntly'', As who should saye the field were mine that daye? {{right|''Gascoigne'', Lookes of a Louer Forsaken.}}}} {{smaller block|The King and Queen enter the Town [Calais] ''triumphantly'', and make their Abode there. {{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 122.}}}} 2†. Festively; rejoicingly. {{smaller block|Dance in Duke Theseus' house ''triumphantly'',
And bless it to all fair prosperity. {{right|''Shak.'', M. N. D., iv. 1. 94.}}}} '''triumpher''' (trī′um-fėr), ''n.'' [< ''triumph'' + ''-er''1.] 1. One who triumphs or rejoices for victory; one who is victorious. {{smaller block|Hee sayd Souldiours were the noblest estate of mankinde, . . . ''triumphers'' both in Camps and Courts. {{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie.}}}} 2. One who was honored with a triumph in Rome. {{smaller block|August was dedicated to Augustus by the senate, because in the same month he was the first time created consul, and thrice ''triumpher'' in Rome. {{right|''Peacham'', On Drawing.}}}} ¶ '''triumphingly''' (trī′um-fing-li), ''adv.'' In a triumphing manner; with triumph or exultation. {{smaller block|''Triumphingly'' say, O Death, where is thy sting? {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Remedy of Discontentment, I. ii. § 1.}}}} '''triumvir''' (trī-um′vėr), ''n.''; pl. ''triumviri'', ''triumvirs'' (-vi-rī, -vėrz). [< L. ''triumvir'', < ''trium'', gen. of ''tres'', three, + ''vir'', man: see ''virile''. Cf. ''duumvir'', ''decemvir''.] One of three men united in office; specifically, in ancient Rome, a member of one of several groups of joint magistrates chosen for various purposes, as for establishing colonies, revising the lists of knights, guarding against fires by night, or to fill various extraordinary commissions on special occasions. {{smaller block|Among the more important of these magistrates were the triumviri capitales, who were elected by the people, and whose duty it was to inquire into capital crimes, to arrest offenders, to superintend the prisons, and to cause the execution of condemned persons. They could punish summarily slaves and persons of the lowest class. See ''triumvirate''.}} {{smaller block|A man may compare Ecbatana of the Medes, Babylon on Euphrates, and Niniue on Tigris, to the ''Triumviri'' at Rome. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 77.}}}} '''triumviral''' (trī-um′vi-ra̤l), ''a.'' [< ''triumvir'' + ''-al.''] Of or pertaining to a triumvir or a triumvirate. {{smaller block|I am about to mount higher than ''triumviral'' tribunal, or than triumphal car. {{right|''Landor'', Imag. Conv., Lucullus and Cæsar.}}}} '''triumvirate''' (trī-um′vi-rāt), ''n.'' [= F. ''triumvirat'' = Pg. ''triumvirato'' = Sp. It. ''triunvirato'', < L. ''triumviratus'', the office or dignity of a triumvir, < ''triumvir'', triumvir: see ''triumvir.''] 1. The office or magistracy of a triumvir, specifically of one of the ancient Roman groups of triumviri.—2. Government by three men in coalition.—3. A group of three men in office or authority; specifically, in ''Rom. hist.'', either the coalition (''First Triumvirate'') between Pompey, Julius Cæsar, and Crassus, 60 {{sc|b. c.}}, which controlled the Roman world for several years, or that (''Second Triumvirate'') between Mark Antony, Octavian (Augustus), and Lepidus, 43 {{sc|b. c.}}, which overthrew the republican party and ordered the second proscription. {{smaller|In the latter Lepidus was soon practically deposed, and Antony and Octavian shared the power until the overthrow of the former, 31 {{sc|b. c.}}}} {{smaller block|Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin were a ''triumvirate'' which governed the country during eight years. {{right|''H. Adams'', Gallatin, p. 274.}}}}
